full_story_part1.text: At the end of a taxi ride or a meal, the payment screen asks one small question: How much would you like to tip? But the screen usually gives an answer first. It shows a few suggested percentages. The first choices may be higher than the amount you planned to give. That first number can change the whole decision. A 2014 study looked at more than 13 million credit card taxi payments in New York City. The researchers found a useful natural test. For fares just below $15 and just above $15, the suggested tip menu changed suddenly. The rides were almost the same price, but some passengers saw a different menu.

full_story_part1.canonical_text:
At the end of a taxi ride or a meal, the payment screen asks one small question:

“How much would you like to tip?”

But the screen usually gives an answer first.

It shows a few suggested percentages. The first choices may be higher than the amount you planned to give. That first number can change the whole decision.

A 2014 study looked at more than 13 million credit card taxi payments in New York City.

The researchers found a useful natural test. For fares just below $15 and just above $15, the suggested tip menu changed suddenly. The rides were almost the same price, but some passengers saw a different menu.

full_story_part2.text: Passengers who saw higher suggested rates left more money. This suggests that the number on the screen can become a starting point. People may begin with that number instead of their own first idea. But there was a catch. When the suggested tip was too high, some customers did not simply choose a smaller amount. They chose zero. So a high default can raise the tip from some customers. But it can also push other customers away from tipping by card completely.

point_one.text: In the United States, restaurant tipping rose from about 10 to 15 percent in the early 1970s to about 20 percent in the late 1990s, according to one policy brief. Digital payment screens can now show tips as high as 35 percent. One expert argues that this changes the feeling of the moment. With a cash tip jar, the choice could be more private. With a screen held by an employee, the customer may feel watched. He calls this pressure guilt tipping.

standard_attempts_log.asr_text: A 2026 survey found that 78% of respondents said tipping had become unreasonable; 44% said they were tipping less than the year before. Among consumers prompted by a digital screen to tip, the share who felt they had to leave a tip fell from 66% in September 2025 to 59% in 2026, and 36% said they chose a custom amount instead of a suggested rate. These are survey answers, not proof that the screen caused the change, but they suggest that many customers are increasingly pushing back against digital prompts to tip.
